title: Running a Marathon
summary: Where the marathon got its name and how runners train, fuel their bodies, drink enough water, and pace themselves to finish a 42-kilometer race.
poll: Anyone can run a marathon if they train well.

versions.title: A Very Long Race
versions.text:
A marathon is a long race. It is so long! It is more than 100 laps of a track. Most folks take four to six hours. The best take just over two.

The race got its name from an old tale. A man ran from a town. The town was named Marathon. He ran all the way to a big city. He had good news to tell.

You can not just get up and run this race. You must train. Some train for months. Each week, they run a bit more. They rest, too. Rest helps their muscles get strong.

You need energy to run. You get it from food like rice and bread. In the race, some run out of it. Their legs feel like stone. They call it "the wall."

You sweat a lot when you run. You lose water. So you need to drink.

Smart runners do not start too fast. They keep a calm speed. That way they can finish.

Big towns hold this race. Riyadh is one. Lots of folks run. Lots more come to cheer!

versions.title: Running a Marathon
versions.text:
A marathon is a long-distance running race. It is 42 kilometers long, which is more than 100 laps around a school track! Most runners take between four and six hours to finish. The fastest runners in the world finish in just over two hours.

The race got its name from an old Greek story. About 2,500 years ago, a messenger is said to have run from a town called Marathon to the city of Athens. He ran to tell people that his army had won a battle. Many experts think the story is partly a legend. Still, it gave people the idea for the first Olympic marathon in 1896.

No one can simply wake up and run a marathon. Runners train for months to build endurance, which means being able to keep going for a long time. Each week, they run a little farther. They also take rest days, because rest gives their muscles time to heal and grow strong.

The body needs energy to keep running for hours. Much of it comes from foods such as rice, bread, and pasta. Late in a race, some runners use up the energy stored in their muscles. Their legs feel heavy and slow. Runners call this "hitting the wall."

Runners also lose water and salt when they sweat. That is why they drink water during the race, most of all on hot days.

Choosing the right pace matters, too. Runners who start too fast often run out of energy early. Wise runners keep a steady pace, so they have enough strength to finish.

Today many big cities, such as Riyadh, hold marathons. Thousands of people run, and many more come to cheer.

versions.title: Running a Marathon
versions.text:
A marathon is a long-distance running race that covers exactly 42.195 kilometers, a distance equivalent to more than 100 laps around a standard school track. Most participants need between four and six hours to finish, whereas the fastest athletes in the world complete the course in just over two hours.

The race takes its name from an ancient Greek story. Approximately 2,500 years ago, a messenger is said to have run from a town called Marathon to the city of Athens to announce that his army had won an important battle. Historians consider the story at least partly a legend, but it nevertheless inspired the first modern Olympic marathon, which was held in Athens in 1896.

Nobody can simply wake up one morning and complete a marathon. Runners usually train for several months to develop endurance, and they gradually increase the length of their runs each week so that their bodies can adapt to the demands of the distance. They also schedule rest days, because recovery gives their muscles time to repair themselves and become stronger.

The body requires an enormous amount of energy to sustain running for hours. Much of that energy comes from carbohydrates in foods such as rice, bread, and pasta, which the body stores in the muscles and liver as a fuel called glycogen. Late in a race, some runners deplete most of their glycogen, and their legs suddenly feel heavy and sluggish, an experience that runners describe as "hitting the wall."

Hydration is equally essential. Runners lose water and salt through sweat, so they drink regularly throughout the race, particularly on hot days.

Finally, a successful marathon requires a sensible strategy. Runners who start too quickly often exhaust their energy prematurely, while experienced runners maintain a consistent pace and conserve strength for the final kilometers.

Today many major cities, including Riyadh, organize marathons. Thousands of people participate, and many more line the streets to encourage them.

versions.title: Running a Marathon
versions.text:
A marathon constitutes a demanding long-distance running competition that covers precisely 42.195 kilometers. This is a considerable distance, roughly equivalent to more than one hundred complete laps around a standard school athletic track. The overwhelming majority of participants require between four and six hours to successfully complete the course. The fastest athletes competing anywhere in the world, by contrast, complete the identical distance in slightly more than two hours. This is an extraordinary athletic accomplishment that demands exceptional physical preparation and remarkable psychological determination in equal measure.

The competition derives its evocative name from an ancient Greek historical narrative. Approximately 2,500 years ago, a messenger is reputed to have run continuously from a settlement called Marathon all the way to the distant city of Athens. His goal was to announce that his army had achieved a significant, decisive military victory. Historians generally consider the underlying story at least partially legendary in nature. It nevertheless inspired the inaugural modern Olympic marathon, which was formally held in Athens during 1896. The precise, standardized distance was only established internationally several subsequent decades afterward.

Nobody can realistically expect to simply awaken one morning and successfully complete a marathon without preparation. Runners typically train for several consecutive months to systematically develop the necessary endurance. They gradually increase the length of their training runs week by week. This allows their cardiovascular systems and muscular tissue sufficient time to adapt progressively to the considerable physiological demands imposed by such an extended distance. They additionally schedule deliberate rest days throughout their training regimen. Adequate recovery provides their muscles with the essential opportunity required to repair microscopic damage and subsequently become progressively stronger over time.

The human body requires an genuinely enormous quantity of metabolic energy to sustain continuous running across several consecutive hours. Much of this essential energy originates from carbohydrates contained within foods such as rice, bread, and pasta. The body subsequently stores this energy within the muscles and liver as a specialized fuel designated glycogen. Late within a race, certain runners deplete the overwhelming majority of their available glycogen reserves. Their legs suddenly feel disproportionately heavy and sluggish, an uncomfortable physiological experience that runners colloquially describe as "hitting the wall" during competition.

Hydration proves equally indispensable throughout the grueling ordeal. Runners lose considerable quantities of water and essential electrolytes, such as salt, through continuous perspiration. They drink fluids regularly throughout the entirety of the race, particularly during hot and humid conditions, when dangerous dehydration can develop with genuinely alarming rapidity and severity.

Finally, successfully completing a marathon requires implementing a sensible, carefully considered strategy from the opening kilometer onward. Competitors who begin running too aggressively frequently exhaust their available energy reserves prematurely. Experienced, seasoned athletes, by contrast, maintain a remarkably consistent pace throughout and deliberately conserve essential strength specifically for the demanding, grueling final kilometers.

Today, many major metropolitan cities, including Riyadh, organize annual marathons, consistently attracting thousands of enthusiastic participants alongside countless cheering spectators who line the streets throughout the course to offer encouragement.

MID.modelAnswer: To build endurance, you should train for several months and run a little farther each week, taking rest days so your muscles can heal. During the race, remember to drink water often, especially on a hot day, since you will sweat and lose both water and salt. Finally, choose a steady pace instead of starting too fast, because runners who sprint early often run out of energy before the finish.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how training, glycogen, hydration, and strategy work together to help a runner finish a marathon. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained at least three of the four ideas.
I showed how the ideas connect to each other.
I used evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Training builds the gradual increase in endurance a runner needs, since running a little farther each week strengthens the muscles enough to handle 42 kilometers. This training also increases how much glycogen, the sugar stored in muscles for fuel, a runner's body can use before it runs out late in the race and causes the feeling known as hitting the wall. Good hydration works alongside this fuel, because runners lose water and salt through sweat, so drinking during the race keeps muscles working properly even as glycogen stores drop. Finally, a smart pacing strategy ties everything together: a runner who starts too fast burns through glycogen and fluids far too quickly, while one who paces steadily uses training, fuel, and hydration efficiently enough to reach the finish line.
